summary: Lists requirements for reliable server pooling, where a group of servers can back each other up and clients can reach a working one. It is the requirements groundwork for protocols of that kind. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If one cashier closes, you walk to another one in line. This writes down what a system needs so that computers can swap in for each other.

subtitle: Requirements for keeping application servers reliably available through pooling.

tldr.problem: Applications need to stay available 24/7 even when servers fail. Proprietary solutions exist, but standards are needed for interoperable, reliable server pooling.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines requirements for an architecture where multiple servers provide the same service, clients can discover healthy ones, and servers can join or leave pools without service interruption.
tldr.outcome: This requirements document guides the design of RSerPool protocols, enabling high-availability deployments of critical applications across different vendors and operating systems.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Architecture for server pool management and client access

facts.label: Key concepts
facts.value: Pool elements, name servers, pool handles, server selection policies

today: RFC 3237 is the foundation for the Reliable Server Pooling architecture. It remains informational, providing the requirements that subsequent RFCs implement. The work has led to protocols such as ASAP (Aggregate Server Access Protocol) and ENRP (Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol) for real deployment.

sections.title: The Problem of Server Availability
sections.content:
The Internet runs continuously, and many businesses depend on services being available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. When a server fails, users expect their applications to keep working by switching to a backup. Today, vendors use proprietary, platform-specific solutions for this.

RFC 3237 defines requirements for an open, standardized approach to reliable server pooling (RSerPool). The goal is to let applications benefit from flexible pooling—where servers join and leave groups, clients find healthy ones, and load is shared—without depending on any single vendor's system.
sections.eli5: Servers fail sometimes. The RFC writes down what an open standard needs to do so anyone can build systems where traffic moves to a working server.

sections.title: The Pooling Architecture
sections.content:
RSerPool introduces several key concepts. A server pool is a group of servers providing the same service. A pool handle (pool name) is a logical identifier for the pool. Pool elements are individual servers registered to the pool. Pool users are clients. A name server keeps track of which pool elements are active in the name space—the part of the network the pooling system covers.

The architecture must work without a single point of failure: if any one name server or pool element fails, others take over. Clients should be able to discover and reach available servers quickly, and the system should handle real-time applications where speed matters.
sections.eli5: There's a list keeper (name server) who knows which cashiers are working. When someone asks 'where can I pay?', the list keeper says 'try cashier 3'. If cashier 3 closes, the list keeper knows, and the next customer goes to cashier 4.

sections.title: Server Registration and Selection
sections.content:
Servers must be able to register with a pool and later deregister without stopping their current work. When a server leaves, clients already connected to it stay connected and finish their business; new clients are sent to other available servers instead.

The architecture must support multiple server selection policies: Round Robin (take turns), Least Used (pick the quietest server), and Most Used (concentration). Clients can even stick with a particular server if it stays alive. Policies must be extensible so new selection methods can be added later.
sections.eli5: Servers can say 'I'm open' or 'I'm closing' without cutting off the people already being served. The system picks which server gets the next customer using rules like 'pick whoever has the fewest people waiting'.

sections.title: Transport and Communication Requirements
sections.content:
RSerPool must work over both TCP and UDP, and must handle the internet reliably. The protocol should not flood the network with overhead traffic even when failures happen. It must follow TCP and SCTP flow control rules, compatible with current Internet practices.

The system should not require multicast, though it can use it if available. Network failures must be handled by the transport layer so applications do not have to deal with them. Finally, the architecture should work on small devices like mobile phones and scale across a range of computing power.
sections.eli5: The messages between the list keeper and the servers must not clog the internet. It should work on old phones and supercomputers alike.

sections.title: Security and Real-time Performance
sections.content:
The RFC requires that attackers cannot impersonate pool elements, deregister servers they do not own, or spoof name server responses. Privacy of client queries must be protected. Name servers must communicate securely with each other just as they do with clients.

For real-time applications, name lookups must be fast, and clients must learn quickly when the pool changes. The system scales to server pools of suitable size—not Internet-wide—so that response times stay bounded. Name servers are organized as a flat group of peers, not hierarchically, keeping updates fast.
sections.eli5: Bad people should not be able to fake being a server. Server lists must stay private. When a new cashier starts, customers should find out quickly, not tomorrow.

sections.title: Applications and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC notes that Reliable Server Pooling benefits both mobile and real-time applications: any service where users expect fast response and high availability. Examples include telecommunications, financial systems, and other mission-critical applications. RSerPool-aware clients get the most benefit, but the architecture should allow non-aware clients to connect too, albeit with less-intelligent server selection.

RFC 3237 is itself only a requirements document; it guides the design of the actual protocols and architecture to come in separate RFCs. Implementation teams use it as the foundation for compatible systems.
sections.eli5: Games, phone systems, banks—anything where being fast and never going down matters—can use this. This RFC says what the real protocol needs to do. Someone else will write the actual recipe.
